title: Let’s Separate What We Know from What We’re Assuming
scene: Your team is discussing why something went wrong, but some explanations are still guesses. You want to separate confirmed facts from assumptions and use evidence to narrow down the possibilities.
sceneJa: チームで問題の原因を話し合っているが、いくつかの説明はまだ推測の段階。分かっている事実と仮説を分け、証拠を使って可能性を絞り込みたい場面。

chunks.en: We have a few possible explanations
chunks.ja: いくつか考えられる説明があります
なぜこれが起きたのかについて

chunks.en: but I think we should separate
chunks.ja: ただ、分けた方がよいと思います
推測していることから
いつ問題が始まったか
そして、どのユーザーに影響があったか
ただ、まだ分かっていません

chunks.en: the most convincing explanation right away,
chunks.ja: 一番もっともらしい説明をすぐに
どんな証拠なら裏付けになるのか
または、それぞれの可能性を除外できるのか
そうすれば〜しやすくなるはずです
入れ込みすぎることなく

questions.question: Which chunking is most natural?
options: separate / what we know / from what we’re assuming
separate what / we know from / what we’re / assuming
separate what we know from what / we’re assuming
questions.explanation: The first version clearly preserves the contrast between ‘what we know’ and ‘what we’re assuming’.

questions.question: What does ‘rule out a possibility’ mean?
questions.explanation: To rule something out means to eliminate it from consideration because the evidence does not support it.

questions.question: Why doesn’t the speaker want to choose the most convincing explanation immediately?
options: Because they want to test each possibility against evidence first
Because they do not need to identify the cause
questions.explanation: The speaker wants evidence to support or eliminate possibilities before becoming attached to one explanation.

speak: Sound curious, not suspicious. Make the contrast in ‘what we know / from what we’re assuming’ clear. Stress the pair ‘support / or rule out’, then slow slightly at ‘without becoming too attached / to one theory’.
review: Previous work-focused session: decide in advance what kind of evidence would justify changing your mind. Useful chunks were ‘what would make us reconsider it’, ‘be willing to adjust the plan’, and ‘strong enough to change our minds’. Today goes one step earlier: before asking what evidence would change your mind, ask what evidence you actually have.
